history.title: טולי והים שבא והולך
history.summary: Tuli, a small sea turtle on the Tel Aviv beach, notices the sea coming and going. Grandma turtle explains that the Moon's gentle pull makes the tides; here the sea moves only a turtle's step, in far places it climbs a giant staircase. Refrain: ששש... הים בא. ששש... הים הולך. Music: Debussy, Clair de lune.

history.title: Mira and the Magnet That Loved Metal
history.summary: Mira, four, is given a little red horseshoe magnet from her grandfather's toolbox. It grabs the spoon and the nail but ignores wood, paper, plastic and glass, and she is afraid it is broken; sorting a click pile and a quiet pile she finds the real rule. The true fact: a magnet only pulls things with iron inside (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt), which is why the aluminium can and the copper coin stay put even though they are metal. Refrain: Click! The magnet grabs. Shhh. The magnet lets go. No music.

history.title: הלב הקטן של תום
history.summary: Tom, four, jumps and dances with Muki the cat before bed, then lies down, feels a fast bum-bum in his chest and is frightened by it. His mother explains that the heart is a muscle about the size of his own fist which sends blood everywhere in the body; it works faster when the muscles ask for more air, and it calms down when he breathes slowly with her. The true fact: heart rate rises with effort and falls at rest, a child's heart beats faster than a grown-up's (and a cat's faster still), and the heart keeps working even during sleep. Refrain: בום־בום. בום־בום. הלב של תום אומר שלום. Music: Brahms, Wiegenlied (Lullaby), sung by Renée Fleming.

music.title: Brahms – Wiegenlied (Lullaby), op. 49 no. 4 (Renée Fleming, Hartmut Höll)

history.title: Sol the Snail and the Silver Trail
history.summary: Sol, a small garden snail, wants to reach the flat board on top of the garden fence to see the first star of the night, but the wood goes straight up and she slides back down and gives up. Nana Snail, old and mossy-shelled, tells her to look behind her at her own long silver trail: her slime holds her like glue when she is still and turns slippery when she pushes, so she practises on a stone and then climbs the post, bit by bit, until she reaches the top and the star. The true fact: a snail's pedal mucus is viscoelastic, gripping like a solid adhesive at rest and flowing like a lubricant under the shear of the foot's muscle waves, which is how snails hold on to vertical walls and still glide forward; most snails move less than about 8 cm a minute. Refrain: Slide and stick. Slide and stick. Little by little, bit by bit. No music.

history.title: האורות הרוקדים בארץ הקרח
history.summary: Sanna, a little girl in a snowy village in the far north, cannot fall asleep on a long winter night, so her grandmother wraps her up and takes her outside into the snow with Nuki, a small reindeer. A thin green line stretches across the sky, widens into a swaying curtain with a soft purple edge, and grandmother explains that it is far higher than the clouds and any aeroplane: tiny sparks fly from the sun, travel a long way, touch the air high above, and the air lights up like a lamp. The true fact: the aurora is made by charged particles from the solar wind striking gases in the upper atmosphere, with its lower edge about 100 km up (a passenger jet flies at only 10-12 km); oxygen glows green and nitrogen blue-purple, and to a watcher it is completely silent. Refrain: אור ירוק. אור סגול. שששש — האורות רוקדים. Music: Sibelius, Valse triste, Turku Philharmonic Orchestra.

music.title: Jean Sibelius – Valse triste, Op. 44 (Turku Philharmonic Orchestra)

history.title: Nina and the Sleepy Violin
history.summary: Nina, four, cannot get Bo her stuffed bear to sleep, and her own loud fast song only keeps him more awake, until Grandpa brings in the small violin he played as a child. He shows her that only the piece of string between her finger and the bow is singing: finger close to the bow makes that piece short and the note high, finger far away makes it long and the note low, and on the fattest string she finds a low soft hum that closes Bo's eyes. The true fact: a vibrating string's pitch is inversely proportional to its length, so pressing a finger shortens the vibrating part and raises the note, while a string's thickness and tension set the pitch of the four open strings (and a cello's strings, about twice as long as a violin's, sound much deeper). Refrain: Long string, low song. Short string, high song. Hmmmm. Music: Saint-Saens, The Swan, Mischa Maisky.

music.title: Camille Saint-Saens - Le Cygne (The Swan) from Le carnaval des animaux (Mischa Maisky, cello; DW Classical Music)

history.title: אדיסון הקטן ואור-הלילה הרך
history.summary: Uri, four and full of questions, cannot fall asleep because his room is either pitch dark or painfully bright. Grandpa Dan tries the big ceiling light (too strong) and a pocket torch (a circle that will not stay put), then brings an old wooden box holding a small glass lamp with a coiled thread inside, and tells him how Edison and his helpers put thread after thread into glass until a scorched cotton thread finally stayed alight for hours and hours. Grandpa sets the little lamp by the bed, its thread glows warm orange, Uri watches his own soft shadow on the wall and falls asleep deciding that tomorrow he will try, and try again, to build a tall tower. The true fact: Edison did not invent the first electric light, but in October 1879 his team found a carbonized cotton thread filament that burned for many hours, and a few months later carbonized bamboo lasted hundreds of hours; the practical part was the whole system he built around it. Refrain: עוד חוט. ועוד חוט. ואז נדלק אור רך.

history.title: Ben and the Green That Was Hiding
history.summary: Ben, four, wants to paint the green frog he found that morning on a wet leaf in the garden, but his three jars hold only red, yellow and blue and he decides his green is missing. Grandma tells him the green is not missing, it is hiding inside the other colours: a blue blob, a yellow blob on top, stirred round and round, and green comes out, then red and yellow make an orange sun and red and blue a purple night sky for the frog to sleep under. The true fact: red, yellow and blue are the painter's traditional primary colours, which cannot be mixed from other paints, while every pigment works by absorbing part of the light and reflecting the rest, so a mixture reflects only what both pigments reflect (subtractive mixing) - blue and yellow leaving green. Refrain: Swish, swish. Swirl, swirl. Come out, colour, come out! No music.

history.title: נופר הדבורה ובית הדבש המושלם
history.summary: Nofar, a young bee, builds her very first honey cells out of hard-won wax and makes them round like the moon; five round rooms later she sees the little empty holes left between them, and is heartbroken that her wax went to waste. Grandma Zehava flies her up to the old comb wall, where Nofar counts the corners of one cell: six, and none of them leave a hole. She rebuilds with six-cornered rooms and discovers that two neighbours share one wall, so the wax stretches further. The true fact: honeycomb cells are hexagons, which tile with no gaps and need the least total wall (the least wax) for a given area - the honeycomb theorem, proved by Thomas Hales in 1999 - while wax is costly, roughly 6-8 kg of honey eaten per kg of wax. Refrain: זמזום, זמזום. שש פינות. ואין חורים. No music.

history.title: Noa and the Stars That Blink
history.summary: Noa, four, goes out on the balcony with her dad before bed and watches one small star shine, go dim and shine again, and is frightened that her star is broken. Her dad explains that the star shines steadily all night long, but its light has to cross the thick moving blanket of air wrapped around the world, where warm and cool layers bend it a tiny step this way and that, so the light wiggles on its way down to her eyes; the moon does not blink because it is a wide disc rather than a pinpoint, so its many wiggles all mix together, and the star low over the rooftops blinks most of all because its light crosses the most air. The true fact: twinkling (scintillation) is added by turbulence in Earth’s atmosphere and not by the star itself, which is why the Moon and the planets look steady and why stars do not twinkle at all seen from above the atmosphere. Refrain: Blink, blink, little light. The star is saying good night. Music: Mozart, 12 Variations on "Ah, vous dirai-je, maman", K. 265, Variation 11 Adagio, played by Isata Kanneh-Mason.

music.title: Mozart - 12 Variations on "Ah, vous dirai-je Maman", K. 265, Var. 11 Adagio (Isata Kanneh-Mason)

history.title: הבלון הרך בתוך גילי
history.summary: Gili, four, jumps and runs right up to bedtime, then lies down and is frightened that his breathing is racing and will not calm down. His mother sits by the bed and stands Dubi, his little teddy, on his tummy: the bear rides up and down fast, and she explains that the belly is like a soft balloon filled and emptied by a wide muscle under the lungs that drops to let air in and rises to push it out. Breathing slowly together, Gili notices that he never told the balloon to slow down - the body does it by itself, fast when he jumps, slow when he rests, and on all night while he sleeps. The true fact: breathing is automatic (the diaphragm contracts and moves down on inhaling, relaxes on exhaling), and the rate falls and becomes very regular on the way into non-REM sleep, reaching its lowest level in deep sleep. Refrain: פנימה, הבלון גדל. החוצה, הבלון קטן. No music.

history.title: Miko the Bat and the Song in the Dark
history.summary: Miko, a young bat, will not leave the cave at night because he cannot see in the dark, and he bumps his wing on a wet rock trying. Mama teaches him her tiny song: he calls out, waits, and the sound touches the wall and comes home to his ears, and she shows him that near things answer fast while far things answer slowly, so the black cave turns into a place full of walls, stones and doorways he can hear. He flies out, clicks his way past a tree and a pond to a moth, and comes home at dawn saying the dark sings back. The true fact: a bat calls and listens to the returning echoes to judge distance and size (echolocation); the calls run from about 14 kHz to over 100 kHz, above the roughly 20 kHz limit of human hearing, and bats are not blind. Refrain: Click, click. Listen. The song comes back. No music.

history.title: מיקה ותם נרדמים על הגל
history.summary: Mika and Tam, two sea otter pups in a cold kelp forest, fall asleep floating on their backs side by side, but the sea drifts them apart in the night and Mika wakes alone on wide grey water; hugging tightly does not survive sleep. Mika's mother lifts a long kelp frond out of the water and shows them it is anchored to the sea floor like a rope, so whoever winds themselves into it stays put, and she joins their paws so they rest close together in the raft. The true fact: sea otters rest on their backs and wrap themselves in kelp or seagrass so the current cannot carry them off while they sleep, they rest in groups called rafts, and a mother wraps her pup in kelp when she dives for food; paw-holding is real but is seen mostly between mother and pup and in aquariums, which the notes for adults flag as the story's one stretch. Refrain: אצה מסביב. כף אל כף. ביחד, ביחד, נרדמים. No music.

history.title: Pip and the Wobbly Tower
history.summary: Pip, a little mouse in a garden shed, wants to reach the small round window where the moon sits, so she ties four sticks into a square and stacks square on square; the tower leans, folds and lies down flat, twice. Grandpa Mo ties three sticks into a triangle, pushes it hard and it does not move, and Pip works out that laying one extra stick across each square, corner to corner, turns it into two triangles that cannot change shape. The true fact: a triangle is the only polygon whose form is fixed by the lengths of its sides, so a four-stick frame with loose corners can rack into a slanted diamond while a triangle cannot, which is why trusses and diagonal bracing fill cranes, roofs, bridges and tall buildings. Refrain: Wibble, wobble, wibble, wobble. Hold still, little tower, hold still. No music.

history.title: קופסת הנגינה של סבתא
history.summary: Ido, four, cannot fall asleep at his grandmother's house because the quiet there is unfamiliar, so she brings down a plain little wooden music box with a small golden key. She winds it, opens the lid, and shows him what is inside: a metal cylinder covered in tiny pins that turns and plucks the teeth of a steel comb, one pin lifting one tooth and letting it spring back into a note, so the tune is written on the cylinder in dots. When the song starts to slow and space out Ido is afraid the box is breaking, and grandmother explains the wound spring whose push is running out, so the box is not broken but tired, like him. The true fact: a music box sounds pins on a rotating cylinder plucking the tuned teeth of a steel comb, driven by a coiled spring whose push finally runs out, which is why the very last notes come slower and quieter. Refrain: דינג, דינג, דינג. הקופסה הקטנה שרה. Music: Satie, Gymnopedie No. 1, Alexandre Tharaud (Warner Classics).

music.title: Erik Satie - Gymnopedie No. 1 (Alexandre Tharaud, piano; Warner Classics)

history.title: Yuval and the Shadow That Grew
history.summary: Yuval, four, wakes in the night, climbs down for a sip of water and freezes: a tall dark giant stands on his bedroom wall and copies every move he makes. Mum sits down on the floor and has him wave, then explains that the little nightlight sends its light out in straight lines which cannot bend around him, so the wall behind him stays dark in his own shape; walking towards the lamp swells the shadow up to the ceiling and walking back to the wall shrinks it to his own size, after which he plays at making a shadow bird, a shadow rabbit and a huge round shadow for Kubi his bear. The true fact: a shadow is a place the light could not reach, and because a nearby lamp's light spreads out in a widening fan, the closer you stand to the lamp the more of that fan you block and the bigger your shadow (roughly your height times the lamp-to-wall distance divided by the lamp-to-you distance); outdoors it does not work, because the Sun is far enough away that its rays arrive almost parallel. Refrain: Step, step, close: the shadow grows tall. Step, step, back: the shadow grows small. No music.

history.title: הירח המתחלף של נועה
history.summary: Noa, four, goes out on the balcony with her mother every evening to find the moon, and over a few nights she watches it lose a piece and thin down to a curved white line, until she is close to tears and sure the moon is finishing. In the dark kitchen her mother lights one side of an orange with a small torch and has her walk slowly around it: the lit part goes from a full circle to a half to a thin bright edge, while the orange never changes at all, and Noa works out that the orange did not shrink, she moved. The true fact: the Sun always lights exactly half the Moon, and because the Moon orbits Earth we see a different amount of that lit half each night, so the phases are a matter of viewing geometry and not of Earth's shadow (that is a lunar eclipse); the Moon makes no light of its own but reflects sunlight, and a full cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days. Refrain: ששש... מסתכלים למעלה. הירח שם. הירח שלם. Music: Beethoven, Moonlight Sonata, first movement, Nikolai Lugansky.

music.title: Beethoven - Piano Sonata no. 14 'Moonlight', I. Adagio sostenuto (Nikolai Lugansky; harmonia mundi)

history.title: Fen the Firefly's Quiet Lamp
history.summary: Fen, a young firefly on her first night of flying, sees the meadow full of fireflies blinking quick bright flashes, but her own lamp will only make one long slow gold glow, so she decides it is broken and hides under her leaf. Her mother has her feel the lamp and find it cool rather than hot, then lifts her own lamp and makes exactly the same long slow glow, explaining that every kind of firefly has its own flash pattern and it is how they say their name in the dark; when Fen glows, slow gold lights answer her from all across the meadow. The true fact: each firefly species has its own flash pattern (how long each flash lasts, how many there are, the pause between them), which is how males signal and females of the same species answer, and a firefly's light is a cold light made by luciferin, oxygen and the enzyme luciferase, giving off almost no heat. Refrain: Blink, blink, quick. Glow, glow, slow. Every little light says hello. No music.

options.title: נור הגמל והדיונה שהולכת לאט
options.summary: A baby camel named Nur worries her favorite sand dune is walking away from her, until Grandpa Camel explains that dunes really do creep forward, grain by grain, so slowly that no one ever sees them move.

options.title: ליאן והמטרייה הראשונה
options.summary: On a rainy night in an old village, Lian learns that people once had only leaves and cloaks to keep dry, until someone coated paper with oil to make the very first waterproof umbrella, and she falls asleep listening to raindrops patter on hers.
options.music: Chopin, Prelude Op. 28 No. 15 "Raindrop" (e.g. Martha Argerich)

options.title: מאיה ומרבד הצבעים של סבתא
options.summary: Maya visits her grandmother's loom on a quiet evening and worries the criss-crossed threads will tangle forever, until she learns the calm over-under rhythm that turns loose strings into a soft, patterned rug.

options.title: נעמה העכבישה סופרת חוטים
options.summary: Na'ama, a young garden spider, wants her web to look exactly like her mother's, so she counts her spokes and spaces them evenly until her web catches the moonlight in a perfect round pattern.

options.title: עומר והפיהוק שרץ לכולם
options.summary: Omer notices his whole family starts yawning right after he does, and his mother explains that a yawn is like a soft, sleepy hello that jumps from one person to the next, cooling tired brains and getting everyone ready for bed.
